<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-grounded cases (A on circadian anchoring plus the 1970s US/Russia reversals; B on a "scheduled vs. unscheduled darkness" asymmetry with a traffic-safety argument). The decisive exchange came in Pressure Questions: A forced B to commit to a concrete threshold ("something like 8:30 is a defensible outer edge") for acceptable winter sunrise under permanent DST. A then used this in Closing to show that Berlin and Warsaw, the very cities B chose to defend, sit an hour past B's own stated line — and B's Closing never squarely answered that arithmetic, instead pivoting back to the schedulable/unschedulable framing without addressing why exceeding its own limit was still tolerable. A also successfully turned B's "collective action" defense of permanent DST back on itself, arguing that if voluntary coordination is too weak to fix evenings under standard time, that same weakness doesn't validate imposing the shift by statute rather than leaving room for local, reversible adaptation (Spain/Germany examples). B's rebuttals were competent and narrowed the debate well, but ultimately left A's "you violated your own standard" attack unresolved, which is the single most damaging blow of the debate. A's Rebuttal 2 being clipped before its final sentence is a minor execution cost, but the substantive A1/A2 answers were intact and the argument was not materially harmed.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Pressure Question forcing B to name a concrete sunrise threshold (8:30), followed by A's Closing showing Berlin/Warsaw exceed that self-imposed line under permanent DST — a concession B's Closing never directly rebutted.</best_rebuttal>
